s0001.literal: Ji in youth was clever and keen, had judgment and capacity, had read widely in histories and annals, and was praised by men of the day.
s0001.idiomatic: As a youth Ji was quick and perceptive, with sound judgment; he had dipped deep into histories and won praise in his day.

s0002.literal: He doffed the commoner's garb as law officer in the establishment of Liang's Prince of Yuzhang.
s0002.idiomatic: His first post was law officer on the staff of Liang's Prince of Yuzhang.

s0003.literal: In Hou Jing's rebellion Ji gathered bold fighters, followed the Founder on campaigns, and by accumulated merit was made Pacifying-Distance General.
s0003.idiomatic: When Hou Jing rebelled Ji raised fighting men and marched with the Founder. Merit piled up until he was made pacifying-distance general.

s0004.literal: When the Founder executed Wang Sengbian, Sengbian's younger brother Sengzhi raised troops and held Wu commandery; the Founder sent Huang Ta at the head of the host to attack him; Sengzhi led troops out at the Xichang Gate to resist; Ta locked with him and could not overcome him.
s0004.idiomatic: After the Founder killed Wang Sengbian, Sengbian's brother Sengzhi seized Wu commandery. The Founder sent Huang Ta with an army against him. Sengzhi marched out the Xichang Gate to fight. Ta held him at bay and could not break him.

s0005.literal: The Founder said to Ji: "The Three Wu are a vital land, of old called rich and fertile; though in the wake of famine and ruin they remain abundant and thriving, yet now the rebels gather and sway the hearts of the realm—without you they cannot be settled. You should think well on your plan.
s0005.idiomatic: The Founder told Ji: "The Three Wu are the empire's rich core. Even after famine they stay prosperous, yet rebels now gather and the realm wavers. No one but you can settle this. Think hard on your plan.

s0006.literal: " Ji then mustered picked troops of his command, marched light and by double stages, went straight from Qiantang toward Wu commandery, Editorial footnote marker 1. and in one night reached below the walls, beat drums, clamored, and pressed the assault.
s0006.idiomatic: " Ji mustered his best troops, traveled light at forced march from Qiantang straight for Wu commandery, [1] and in a single night was under the walls beating drums and storming the gate.

s0007.literal: Sengzhi suspected a great army had come, fled in a light boat to Du Kan, and Ji entered and held the commandery.
s0007.idiomatic: Sengzhi thought a great host had arrived, fled by light boat to Du Kan, and Ji entered and took the commandery.

s0008.literal: The Founder commended him and memorialized him appointed Administrator of Wu commandery.
s0008.idiomatic: The Founder praised him and memorialized his appointment as administrator of Wu commandery.

s0009.literal: When the Founder received the Mandate, Ji was summoned as Left Guard General.
s0009.idiomatic: When the Founder took the throne Ji was summoned as left guard general.

s0010.literal: At the beginning of Tiancheng he went out as Bearer of the Staff and Interior Minister of Nankang.
s0010.idiomatic: At the opening of Tiancheng (560) he was sent out as bearer of the staff and interior minister of Nankang.

s0011.literal: At that time Zhang Shaobin, Administrator of Yian, held the commandery in rebellion; Emperor Wen made Ji Bearer of the Staff and Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs in the North of the Range, and he led the host to campaign and pacify him.
s0011.idiomatic: Zhang Shaobin, administrator of Yian, rebelled and held his commandery. Emperor Wen made Ji bearer of the staff and commander of the armies north of the range, and he led troops to crush him.

s0012.literal: On his return he was removed and made Scattered Cavalry Regular Attendant and Left Chief Clerk of the Secretariat.
s0012.idiomatic: Returning, he was made scattered-cavalry regular attendant and left chief clerk of the Secretariat.

s0013.literal: In the fifth year he was given Cloud-Banner General and Chamberlain for the Palace, enfeoffed as Marquis of Dongxing county with a fief of six hundred households.
s0013.idiomatic: In the fifth year he was made cloud-banner general and chamberlain for the palace, and enfeoffed as Marquis of Dongxing with six hundred households.

s0014.literal: When Hua Jiao raised troops upriver, Emperor Xuan was then Recorder of the Secretariat assisting in government; he ordered all armies out to campaign and entrusted Ji with overall command of inner and outer city defense and military affairs.
s0014.idiomatic: When Hua Jiao rebelled upriver, Emperor Xuan was regent as recorder of the Secretariat. He sent every army against Jiao and put Ji in charge of all city defenses, within and without.

s0015.literal: When Jiao was pacified, Emperor Xuan took the throne; in the first year of Taijian he was given Administrator of Dongyang, changed in enfeoffment to Marquis of Le'an county with a fief of one thousand households.
s0015.idiomatic: After Jiao fell, Emperor Xuan succeeded. In Taijian year 1 (569) Ji was made administrator of Dongyang and re-enfeoffed as Marquis of Le'an with one thousand households.

s0016.literal: In the fourth year he entered office as Grand Steward.
s0016.idiomatic: In the fourth year he entered court as grand steward.

s0017.literal: In the fifth year he was transferred to Minister of Justice.
s0017.idiomatic: In the fifth year he was transferred to minister of justice.

s0018.literal: Wu Mingche commanded the armies on the northern campaign; an edict ordered Ji in his present office to oversee Mingche's army.
s0018.idiomatic: Wu Mingche led the northern campaign. An edict made Ji, in his existing post, overseer of Mingche's army.

s0019.literal: When Huainan was pacified he was given Army Master General and Inspector of Yu.
s0019.idiomatic: When Huainan was pacified he was made army-master general and inspector of Yu.

s0020.literal: Ji was skilled at soothing and gathering; he won the people's harmony exceedingly.
s0020.idiomatic: Ji was skilled at winning people over and enjoyed deep goodwill among them.

s0021.literal: He was reassigned Bearer of the Staff and Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs in Qiao province and Inspector of Qiao.
s0021.idiomatic: He was reassigned bearer of the staff, commander of Qiao province, and inspector of Qiao.

s0022.literal: Before he could take up the post, Mingche received orders to advance and campaign against Peng and Bian; Ji was made commander and advanced with Mingche in pincer.
s0022.idiomatic: Before he took up office, Mingche was ordered to strike Peng and Bian. Ji was made commander and marched in pincer with him.

s0023.literal: The army was defeated at Lüliang and fell into Zhou; Zhou made him Senior Opening General.
s0023.idiomatic: The army was broken at Lüliang and he fell into Zhou hands. Zhou made him senior opening general.

s0024.literal: In the fourteenth year of Sui's Kaihuang era he died at Chang'an, aged seventy-three.
s0024.idiomatic: In Kaihuang year 14 of Sui (594) he died at Chang'an, aged seventy-three.

s0025.literal: Sun Yang, styled Delian, was a native of Wu in Wu commandery.
s0025.idiomatic: Sun Yang, styled Delian, came from Wu in Wu commandery.

s0026.literal: His grandfather Wenhui was Qi Colonel of the Yue Cavalry and Administrator of Qingyuan.
s0026.idiomatic: His grandfather Wenhui had been Qi colonel of the Yue cavalry and administrator of Qingyuan.

s0027.literal: His father Xundao, Editorial footnote marker 2. was Liang Palace Attendant and was famed for refined simplicity.
s0027.idiomatic: His father Xundao [2] was a Liang palace attendant, known for refined simplicity.

s0028.literal: Yang in youth was free and bold, loved strategy, read widely in the classics and histories, and was especially skilled at letters.
s0028.idiomatic: As a youth Yang was bold and fond of strategy; he read widely in the classics and histories and excelled at correspondence.

s0029.literal: He began his career as acting aide in the light-chariot service of Liang's Heir of Linchuan, and was promoted in succession to water-and-arms clerk in the military staff of the Prince of Shao-ling, Pacifier of the West.
s0029.idiomatic: He entered service as acting aide to Liang's Heir of Linchuan in the light-chariot office, then rose to water-and-arms clerk on the military staff of the Prince of Shao-ling, pacifier of the west.

s0030.literal: When the prince went out to garrison Yingzhou, Yang moved his whole household with the headquarters and was greatly favored.
s0030.idiomatic: When the prince took up his post at Yingzhou, Yang brought his whole household to the headquarters and won high favor.

s0031.literal: In the turmoil of Taiping he was given acting staff, made Fierce Martial General, and made army commander.
s0031.idiomatic: In the Taiping turmoil he received acting credentials as fierce-martial general and army commander.

s0032.literal: When Wang Sengbian campaigned against Hou Jing, Wang Lin was vanguard; Lin and Yang were of the same gate, and Lin memorialized recommending him as Martial-Announcements General and Administrator of Yidu, and he followed Sengbian to rescue Xu Wensheng at Wuchang.
s0032.idiomatic: When Wang Sengbian attacked Hou Jing, Wang Lin led the van. Lin and Yang were schoolmates; Lin recommended him as martial-announcements general and administrator of Yidu, and he followed Sengbian to relieve Xu Wensheng at Wuchang.

s0033.literal: When Yingzhou fell he remained with the army to garrison Baling and repaired preparations for battle and defense.
s0033.idiomatic: When Yingzhou fell he stayed behind to hold Baling and strengthened its defenses.

s0034.literal: Soon Hou Jing's troops arrived and attacked day and night; Yang supervised his command in full strength to resist; the rebel host broke and fled.
s0034.idiomatic: Soon Hou Jing's troops came and besieged him day and night. Yang led his men in a full defense and drove the rebels back.

s0035.literal: Yang followed the great army downriver; when Guni was taken Yang fought hard with merit; he was removed and made Supernumerary Scattered Cavalry Regular Attendant, enfeoffed Marquis of Fuyang county with a fief of one thousand households.
s0035.idiomatic: He followed the main fleet downstream. At the taking of Guni he fought with distinction and was made supernumerary scattered-cavalry regular attendant and Marquis of Fuyang with one thousand households.

s0036.literal: Soon he was given acting staff, made Trustworthy Faith General and Interior Minister of Hengyang; before he could take up the post he was transferred to marshal of the Pacify-the-South headquarters in Heng province.
s0036.idiomatic: Soon he received acting staff as trustworthy-faith general and interior minister of Hengyang. Before he took office he was made marshal of the pacify-the-south headquarters in Heng province.

s0037.literal: For merit in breaking the Yellow-Cave Man rebels he was removed and made Administrator of Dongguan, acting Administrator of Guangzhou.
s0037.idiomatic: For breaking the Yellow-Cave rebels he was made administrator of Dongguan and acting administrator of Guangzhou.

s0038.literal: Soon he was removed and made Intelligent Martial General and overseer of Xiang province affairs.
s0038.idiomatic: Soon he was made intelligent-martial general and overseer of Xiang province.

s0039.literal: When the Honored Emperor succeeded he was given staff, made Benevolent Prestige General, and Administrator of Ba.
s0039.idiomatic: When the Honored Emperor succeeded he received the staff as benevolent-prestige general and administrator of Ba.

s0040.literal: When the Founder received the Mandate, Wang Lin set up Liang's Prince of Yongjia Xiao Zhuang at Yingzhou; Yang was summoned as Grand Steward, Editorial footnote marker 3. and promoted to Direct Communication Scattered Cavalry Regular Attendant.
s0040.idiomatic: When the Founder took the throne, Wang Lin enthroned Liang's Prince of Yongjia Xiao Zhuang at Yingzhou. Yang was summoned as grand steward [3] and promoted to direct-communication scattered-cavalry regular attendant.

s0041.literal: When Wang Lin invaded, Yang was made Bearer of the Staff, Scattered Cavalry Regular Attendant, Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs in the five provinces of Ying, Jing, Ba, Wu, and Xiang, Pacifying-the-West General, and Inspector of Ying, with overall charge of the rear headquarters.
s0041.idiomatic: When Wang Lin invaded, Yang was made bearer of the staff, scattered-cavalry regular attendant, commander of Ying, Jing, Ba, Wu, and Xiang, pacifying-the-west general and inspector of Ying, with full charge of the rear headquarters.

s0042.literal: Zhou sent the great general Shi Ning at the head of forty thousand men, who came by surprise in force; Yang's assistant defender Zhang Shi [Gui] raised the outer city to welcome them, Editorial footnote marker 4. and there were lost among soldiers and people, men and women, more than three thousand persons.
s0042.idiomatic: Zhou sent the great general Shi Ning with forty thousand men in a sudden rush. Yang's assistant defender Zhang Shi [Gui] opened the outer city to them. [4] More than three thousand soldiers and civilians, men and women, were lost.

s0043.literal: The Zhou army again raised earthen hills and high ladders and attacked day and night; they took advantage of the wind to set fire and burned more than fifty towers on the inner city's south face.
s0043.idiomatic: The Zhou army raised siege mounds and scaling ladders and pressed day and night. They used the wind to fire the inner city's southern face and burned more than fifty towers.

s0044.literal: At that time Yang's troops were fewer than a thousand; he manned the walls to resist; Yang personally went about encouraging them, walking the ramparts with wine and food; the soldiers all fought to the death for him.
s0044.idiomatic: Yang had fewer than a thousand men. He held the walls himself, walking the battlements with wine and food. Every soldier fought for him to the last.

s0045.literal: The Zhou men attacked bitterly and could not overcome him; they then falsely invested him as Pillar of State, Inspector of Ying, and Duke of a Ten-Thousand-Household Commandery.
s0045.idiomatic: The Zhou attacked hard and failed. They then falsely invested him as pillar of state, inspector of Ying, and duke of a ten-thousand-household commandery.

s0046.literal: Yang pretended to agree to gain time, while secretly repairing war gear; towers, parapets, and engines were in one morning set in strict array; the Zhou men greatly feared him.
s0046.idiomatic: Yang feigned acceptance to buy time while secretly readying arms. Towers, parapets, and engines stood complete by morning, and the Zhou were deeply afraid.

s0047.literal: When he heard the great army had defeated Wang Lin and was advancing in victory, the Zhou troops then lifted the siege.
s0047.idiomatic: When word came that the main army had broken Wang Lin and was marching in triumph, the Zhou lifted the siege.

s0048.literal: Yang then held all the midstream lands; he gathered his generals and said to them: "I and the princes exerted strength together in righteousness and jointly upheld the house of Liang—we have already toiled enough.
s0048.idiomatic: Yang then held the entire mid-Yangzi. He assembled his officers and said: "We served the princes in righteousness and upheld Liang together. We have labored long enough.

s0049.literal: Now the times are thus—can Heaven be defied!
s0049.idiomatic: The times stand as they do. Who defies Heaven?

s0050.literal: " He then sent envoys with a memorial to the court.
s0050.idiomatic: " He sent envoys with a memorial to court.

s0051.literal: In the first year of Tiancheng he was given Bearer of the Staff, Scattered Cavalry Regular Attendant, Pacifying-the-South General, and Inspector of Xiang, enfeoffed Marquis of Dingxiang county with a fief of one thousand households.
s0051.idiomatic: In Tiancheng year 1 (560) he was made bearer of the staff, scattered-cavalry regular attendant, pacifying-the-south general and inspector of Xiang, and enfeoffed as Marquis of Dingxiang with one thousand households.

s0052.literal: Yang was uneasy at heart and firmly asked to enter court; he was summoned as Scattered Cavalry Regular Attendant and Central Army Commander.
s0052.idiomatic: Yang could not rest easy and begged to come to court. He was summoned as scattered-cavalry regular attendant and central army commander.

s0053.literal: Editorial footnote marker 5. Before he took the appointment, Emperor Wen spoke to Yang at ease and said: "Of old Zhu Maichen wished to be magistrate of his home commandery—do you have such a wish?
s0053.idiomatic: [5] Before he took office, Emperor Wen said to him gently: "Zhu Maichen once longed to govern his home commandery. Do you feel the same?

s0054.literal: " He was thereupon reassigned Bearer of the Staff, Pacifying-the-East General, and Administrator of Wu commandery, and given one set of martial pipes and drums.
s0054.idiomatic: " He was then made bearer of the staff, pacifying-the-east general, and administrator of Wu commandery, with a suite of martial pipes and drums.

s0055.literal: When he was about to go to his post the imperial carriage came to the near suburbs to see him off and feast him; his home district was glorified.
s0055.idiomatic: As he set out for his post the emperor's carriage came to the near suburbs to feast and send him off. His home district took it as glory.

s0056.literal: When his term ended he was summoned and appointed Scattered Cavalry Regular Attendant and Central Guard Commander, martial pipes and drums as before.
s0056.idiomatic: When his term ended he was recalled as scattered-cavalry regular attendant and central guard commander, keeping his pipes and drums.

s0057.literal: When Liu Yi rebelled in Dongyang an edict ordered Yang to command the river fleet in advance to campaign.
s0057.idiomatic: When Liu Yi rebelled in Dongyang an edict put Yang in command of the river fleet to attack him.

s0058.literal: When Yi was pacified he was transferred to General Who Guards the Right, regular attendant and martial pipes and drums unchanged.
s0058.idiomatic: After Yi was crushed he was made general who guards the right, retaining his attendant post and pipes and drums.

s0059.literal: Before long he went out as Bearer of the Staff, Pacifying-the-East General, and Administrator of Jian'an.
s0059.idiomatic: Soon he was sent out as bearer of the staff, pacifying-the-east general, and administrator of Jian'an.

s0060.literal: In the Guangda era he was removed for public business; soon he was raised again as Direct Communication Scattered Cavalry Regular Attendant.
s0060.idiomatic: In the Guangda era (567) he was dismissed on official grounds, then soon restored as direct-communication scattered-cavalry regular attendant.

s0061.literal: When Emperor Xuan took the throne, because Yang's achievement and fame had long been outstanding, he deeply entrusted affairs to him.
s0061.idiomatic: When Emperor Xuan succeeded, Yang's record and fame were already great, and the emperor relied on him heavily.

s0062.literal: In the fourth year of Taijian he was given command of military affairs in Jing and Xin provinces, made Pacifying-the-West General and Inspector of Jing, and went out to garrison Gong'an.
s0062.idiomatic: In Taijian year 4 (572) he was made commander of Jing and Xin, pacifying-the-west general and inspector of Jing, and marched out to hold Gong'an.

s0063.literal: Yang further repaired the walls and moats, won over the distant borders, and was feared by neighboring territories.
s0063.idiomatic: He strengthened walls and moats, won over distant peoples, and neighboring states feared him.

s0064.literal: After six years in office he was again removed for an affair and made Direct Communication Scattered Cavalry Regular Attendant once more.
s0064.idiomatic: After six years in post he was dismissed again on official grounds and returned as direct-communication scattered-cavalry regular attendant.

s0065.literal: When Wu Mingche's army was defeated at Lüliang he was given Bearer of the Staff and command of river and land forces along the frontier, made General Who Guards the West, and given one set of martial pipes and drums.
s0065.idiomatic: When Wu Mingche was broken at Lüliang he was made bearer of the staff, commander of frontier river and land forces, general who guards the west, with a suite of pipes and drums.

s0066.literal: Soon he was given Scattered Cavalry Regular Attendant and command of military affairs in the five provinces of Jing, Ying, Ba, Wu, and Xiang, and Inspector of Ying; staff, general, and martial pipes and drums were as before.
s0066.idiomatic: Soon he was scattered-cavalry regular attendant, commander of Jing, Ying, Ba, Wu, and Xiang, and inspector of Ying, keeping staff, rank, and pipes and drums.

s0067.literal: In the twelfth year he was punished for trafficking at the frontier.
s0067.idiomatic: In the twelfth year he was punished for illicit dealings on the border.

s0068.literal: When the Last Emperor succeeded he was again removed and made Direct Communication Scattered Cavalry Regular Attendant, concurrently Minister for Founding Works.
s0068.idiomatic: When the Last Emperor succeeded he was again made direct-communication scattered-cavalry regular attendant and concurrent minister for founding works.

s0069.literal: Soon he was removed and made Central Guard Commander, his noble rank and fief restored; he entered office as Minister of Revenue and led the Footsoldiers Commandant.
s0069.idiomatic: Soon he was made central guard commander with rank and fief restored, then minister of revenue and leader of the footsoldiers commandant.

s0070.literal: Before long he was added Scattered Cavalry Regular Attendant and transferred to Palace Attendant and Minister of the Ancestral Temples.
s0070.idiomatic: Before long he was added scattered-cavalry regular attendant, then made palace attendant and minister of the ancestral temples.

s0071.literal: The Last Emperor often visited his residence, and composed poems and rhapsodies describing the beauty of his achievements, displaying the affection between ruler and minister.
s0071.idiomatic: The Last Emperor often visited his house and wrote poems and rhapsodies praising his merit, showing the warmth between throne and subject.

s0072.literal: He was again made Minister of the Five Arms and led the Right Army General, Editorial footnote marker 6. palace attendant as before.
s0072.idiomatic: He was again made minister of the five arms and leader of the right army general, [6] retaining his palace attendant post.

s0073.literal: Because of old age he repeatedly begged to retire on account of infirmity; gracious edicts would not permit it.
s0073.idiomatic: Age wore on him and he repeatedly asked leave to retire; gracious edicts refused.

s0074.literal: In the first year of Zhenming he died in office, aged seventy-two.
s0074.idiomatic: In Zhenming year 1 (587) he died in office, aged seventy-two.

s0075.literal: The Last Emperor came in person to mourn and wept with utmost grief; posthumously he was given General Who Guards the Army, palace attendant as before, one set of martial pipes and drums, one set of court robes, one suit of garments; funeral rites were supplied in generous measure according to the occasion; his posthumous title was Huanzi.
s0075.idiomatic: The Last Emperor came in person to mourn with deepest grief. He was posthumously made general who guards the army, palace attendant as before, with pipes and drums, court robes, and a suit of garments; funeral costs were generously supplied; his posthumous title was Huanzi.

s0077.literal: Yang served his parents with filial fame and was deeply affectionate toward his younger brothers.
s0077.idiomatic: Yang was known for filial service to his parents and deep affection for his younger brothers.

s0078.literal: By nature he was open and easy; he had wealth and goods and gave them away to kin and friends.
s0078.idiomatic: He was open-handed by nature and gave his wealth freely to kin and friends.

s0079.literal: In his own dwelling he rather failed in extravagance and pride; courtyards were dug through and built up to the utmost of forest and spring charm; singing bells and dancing girls were rare in the age; guests filled his gate and lofty carriages never ceased.
s0079.idiomatic: His own household leaned toward luxury: courtyards were terraced into gardens to the limit of woodland and spring beauty; singing bells and dancing girls were seldom matched in the age; guests packed his gate and fine carriages never stopped coming.

s0080.literal: When he went out to garrison Yingzhou he joined more than ten boats into a great barge; within it he set up a pavilion and pool and planted lotus and water chestnuts; on every fine day of good scenery officials and guests all gathered, set wine while drifting on the long river—it was also a splendor of the time.
s0080.idiomatic: When he held Yingzhou he lashed more than ten boats into a great barge with a pavilion and pool inside and lotus planted about it. On fair days he gathered guests and officers, floated the long Yangzi with wine set out—a wonder of the age.

s0081.literal: He often set up a lecture hall in his mountain studio, gathered scholars of the profound learning, and supported them winter and summer; scholars praised him.
s0081.idiomatic: He often held a lecture hall in his mountain retreat, gathered learned men, and supported them winter and summer; scholars praised him for it.

s0082.literal: Yet in his own conduct he was easy and direct and did not treat others with arrogance because of name and rank.
s0082.idiomatic: Yet in his own bearing he was plain and never looked down on others because of rank.

s0083.literal: At that time Master Lang of Xinghuang Temple had thoroughly mastered the Buddhist canon, Editorial footnote marker 8. and whenever Yang came to the lecture seat there was debate; the community of the Law all turned their hearts to him.
s0083.idiomatic: Master Lang of Xinghuang Temple had mastered the Buddhist canon. [8] Whenever Yang came to the lecture hall they argued points, and the monastic community hung on his words.

s0084.literal: He was also surpassing in ingenious thought; as Minister for Founding Works he created many of the army's and state's engines and gear.
s0084.idiomatic: His ingenuity surpassed others. As minister for founding works he devised much of the army's and state's equipment.

s0085.literal: He had discernment; in marriages for sons and daughters he always chose families of plain nobility.
s0085.idiomatic: He had a keen eye; for his children's marriages he always chose families of quiet distinction.

s0086.literal: When he died, Secretariat Director Jiang Zong composed his funerary inscription; the Last Emperor also inscribed forty characters after the inscription and sent Left Household Minister Cai Zheng with an edict to his residence to carve it.
s0086.idiomatic: When he died, Secretariat Director Jiang Zong wrote his epitaph. The Last Emperor added forty characters of his own and sent Left Household Minister Cai Zheng with an edict to carve them at Yang's house.

s0087.literal: The words read: "Autumn wind stirs bamboo; misty waters startle the waves.
s0087.idiomatic: The text runs: "Autumn wind stirs the bamboo; misted waters startle the waves.

s0088.literal: How many men on the woodcutters' path—where is that mountain slope?
s0088.idiomatic: How many men on the woodcutters' path—where is that mountain slope?

s0089.literal: The sun and moon of today—the brocade and gauze of nights past.
s0089.idiomatic: Today's sun and moon—the brocade and gauze of nights gone by.

s0090.literal: Heaven long, the road far; earth enduring, clouds many.
s0090.idiomatic: Heaven is long and the road far; earth endures and clouds are many.

s0091.literal: Meritorious ministers not yet inscribed—what of this intent?
s0091.idiomatic: Merit not yet carved in stone—what shall we make of this heart?

s0092.literal: " Men of the time held it an honor.
s0092.idiomatic: " Men of the time took it as glory.

s0093.literal: Yang had twenty-one sons; all had their father's manner.
s0093.idiomatic: Yang had twenty-one sons, each with his father's bearing.

s0095.literal: The second son Xun was rather famed; he served in succession as magistrate of Linxiang, Direct-Gate General, and Administrator of Gaotang.
s0095.idiomatic: The second son Xun won some fame as magistrate of Linxiang, direct-gate general, and administrator of Gaotang.

s0096.literal: When Chen perished he entered Sui.
s0096.idiomatic: When Chen fell he entered Sui service.

s0098.literal: The historiographer says: In the last years of Liang, bandits and rebels were truly numerous; the Founder raised righteousness and bore the standard, about to bring peace to the realm; Pei Ji early recognized whom to follow and was always in the military entourage; [smash] the enemy's edge and drive them back, Editorial footnote marker 9. he achieved merit many times.
s0098.idiomatic: The historiographer writes: In Liang's last years rebels swarmed. The Founder raised the banner of righteousness to pacify the realm. Pei Ji saw early whom to follow and was ever in the field, [smashing] the enemy's van and driving them back [9] again and again.

s0099.literal: Sun Yang had civil and military capacity and plan, was known to the ruler of the age; in marching armies and using troops he followed the methods of the Marshal; as to defeating the enemy in battle and taking by assault, he repeatedly achieved merit and fame; moreover he loved giving and received people well—officers and men all admired and turned to him.
s0099.idiomatic: Sun Yang had civil and military talent and won his sovereign's trust. In command he followed the marshal's art; in battle he took cities and won repeated glory. He was generous and approachable, and soldiers admired him.

s0100.literal: Yet by nature he did not keep to constancy and was repeatedly removed for crimes—he was perhaps of Chen Tang's kind.
s0100.idiomatic: Yet he was not steady by nature and was often dismissed for fault—perhaps a man in Chen Tang's mold.
